newsitem.title: POLAND: FORECAST - LODZ INSTITUTE POLISH MID-TERM FORECAST.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - LODZ INSTITUTE POLISH MID-TERM FORECAST.

text.p: Following is a macroeconomic mid-term economic forecast by
Poland's independent Lodz Institute of Forecasts and Economic
Analyses (LIFEA) contributed to Reuters.
DOMESTIC DEMAND DRIVES ECONOMY IN FIRST HALF OF 1996
Economic growth, especially in industry, continued but at a
slower pace and the rate of inflation dropped close to official
target figures.
Major growth factors became components of final domestic
demand: investment and private consumption, replacing exports
as the engine of economic growth.
For the first year since the start of reform in 1990 net
exports will decline due to slow down of growth rates of
commodity exports related to the decline in the economic
climate in the European Union, especially Germany.
It is also due to a postponed recovery of the East European
countries and the real appreciation of zloty against the
dollar. The rise of the zloty also caused the rapid growth of
imports, stimulated additionally by an increase of agricultural
imports amid declining domestic crop output.
GDP GROWTH SEEN BELOW GOVERNMENT 6 PCT TARGET
The above mentioned factors will contribute to the decline
of the growth rate of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in 1996 to
5.2 percent, less than the official target of six percent. The
private sector will grow more quickly than the public sector.
Overall growth will be constrained by a moderate harvest in
agriculture struck by unfavourable weather conditions in the
winter and spring. Sustained economic growth will bring a
moderate net increase in the number of jobs and a small decline
in the unemployment rate (from an average 14.9 percent in 1995
to 14.4 percent in 1996).
Construction output will recover in the second half of the
year from a drop-off in the first half due to the harsh winter.
We expect the average rate of inflation in 1996 will be
over 21 percent. Money supply will follow the money demand
constrained by the high interest rates, which will decline
rather slowly.
State budget revenues will increase by two to three percent
in real terms. As budget expenditures are limited, the deficit
will stay at the low 2.8 to 2.9 percent of the GDP, as it has
done in previous years.
External conditions are assumed to improve in 1997 and the
following years, including GDP growth and trade with the EU, as
well as the expected recovery of the East European trade
partners.
One should emphasise the growing interest of foreign
investors to invest in Poland. The manufacturing costs remain
low compared to developed market economies while the legal and
security conditions steadily improve.
We assume that the policy of slowing inflation and
promotion of economic growth will be continued in coming years,
as written in the official government program -- Package 2000.
3. SUMMARY, 1997 AND BEYOND
The forecast for the year 1997 and the next several years
was elaborated using a modified W5 version, annual
macroeconometric model of the national economy of Poland.
GDP
The forecast long-term rate of GDP growth will be around
five percent per year. We predict 5.6 percent growth in 1997
close to the government's target. The major source of growth in
the next years will remain investment and private consumption.
By the end of century once again Polish trade balance will
become positive if further real appreciation of zloty is
avoided.
INVESTMENT
The rate of growth of investment outlays is forecasted to
decline from an exceptionally high level in 1995 and 1996, at
around 15 percent, to their long-term levels, around 11 percent
in 1997 and around 10 percent until 1999 (the rates of growth
of machinery equipment investment will be much higher).
This allows for positive growth expectations resulting from
declining risks in financing investment activities and
investment promotion by government institutions and banks.
A recovery in housing investment is also expected as early
as 1997, which will increase the rates of growth of investment
in construction.
CONSUMPTION
Private consumption growth is high, approaching five
percent in 1997 and moderately declining to around four percent
in the next several years. The high rates of growth are
stimulated by the quick development of consumer credit use,
especially for cars, furniture, other household equipment.
EXPORTS
The forecasted growth rates of commodity exports are high,
but steadily declining from the second half of 1995 to an
expected nine percent in 1997.
During the next several years it will still be one of the
main driving forces positively affecting structural changes of
the Polish economy in transition.
The decline of the rate of growth of exports is mainly the
result of the expected real appreciation of zloty. Commodity
imports are forecasted to increase by roughly 14 percent in
1997 and by between 12 and 9 percent in the next years.
For the above reasons the balance of trade in the year 1997
will be negative (estimated at some $11 billion) and in the
next several years will continue to deteriorate.
INDUSTRIAL OUTPUT
The demand for industrial goods will show high growth rates
in value added terms.
It will grow by six percent in 1997 and decline in the next
few years to five percent. The building industry will also show
high rates of growth declining from eight percent in 1997 to
six percent by 1999.
AGRICULTURE AND UNEMPLOYMENT
Agriculture output is forecasted to grow at a moderate
three to four percent, except for 1997 when it should recover
from a poor 1996 with seven percent growth.
These rates of growth are associated with a modest increase
in employment from 1.1 percent in 1997 to 1.5 percent by the
end of century.
This means, that with a very moderate increase in the
supply of labour the overall number of jobless will decline
from (an average of) 2.4 million in 1997 to 2.2 million in 1999
and average rate of unemployment from 14 percent in 1997 to
12.6 percent in 1999.
INFLATION AND THE BUDGET
The rates of inflation will decline over the forecast
horizon. We forecast for 1997 an average increase of retail
prices of consumer goods to be 18 percent and less than 10
percent in 1999. This forecast is on the lower end of the
expected growth of the rate of inflation as it assumes no
serious demand pressures.
The 1997 state budget will probably once again be non
expansionist. In effect, the budget deficit is estimated at
more than 10 billion zloty, or about 2.6 to 2.7 percent of GDP.
If this budget policy is continued, then the budget
deficit/GDP ratio will show a declining tendency approaching
1.9 percent by the end of the century.
5. POLICY ISSUES AND UNCERTAINTIES
The last two years, being extremely good as far as rates of
growth are concerned, need not be an exception. Reaching high
rates of growth of between seven and nine percent still is
feasible.
We must repeat that there are resources which are not fully
utilised, such as fixed capital as well as high unemployment.
On the other hand, the involvement of foreign capital in
the investment activities could be larger than before. This
would require, however, more aggresive promotion of exports,
including real depreciation of the zloty and a more
expansionist financial policy.
The high rates of GDP growth might be also supported by the
continuation of high investment activities.
The announced changes in tax policy aimed at gradually
reducing the income tax rates might increase the propensity to
save in the household and business sector, thus increasing
investments.
The wages, expressed in dollar terms, are still low, but
the labour force is well educated. These factors make us
believe that in the medium-term foreign direct investment will
grow at higher rates than before, taking into account declining
risks.
The perspectives for further export expansion as seen in
the far-East seem to be seriously endangered because of the
conservative monetary policy. Also further appreciation of the
zloty may cause the deterioration of financial prospects for
the Polish exporters.
